Constitution, By-Laws and University Manual Committee Report # 2020-2021-4 to the Faculty Senate Faculty Senate Meeting, April 15, 2021 Accelerated Bachelor's and Master's degree UM Revised Language 3.30.10 The Graduate School. The University offers programs leading to Accelerated Bachelor's and Master's of Arts or Seienee degrees (ABM), Master of Arts or Science degrees, professional master's and doctoral degrees and the Doctor of Philosophy degree, in cooperation with the colleges. Degree requirements are described in the Graduate School Manual. #16-17-18 3.30.11 The Dean of the Graduate School shall have primary responsibility for administering the policies and procedures of graduate study. 3.30.12 The Dean is a member of the Graduate Faculty per 4.70.10 and shall be a non-voting ex officio member of the Graduate Council. The Dean shall be the executive officer of the Graduate Faculty. #19-20-30 3.30.13 The Dean shall transmit to the Faculty Senate actions of the Graduate Council and/or Graduate Faculty, as specified in Sections 5.65.30-5.65.37, requiring its approval; administer and enforce regulations pertaining to the conduct of graduate student work and the granting of graduate degrees and certify to the Graduate Council the names of students who have satisfied requirements for degrees; administer the executive office of the Graduate School, maintain appropriate records, prepare the annual budget, make regular reports to the President and to the Graduate Faculty on the condition

of the Graduate School; and perform other related duties necessary for the effective functioning of the Graduate School. #19-20-30 3.30.14 Early in each academic year, the Dean shall update the list of the Graduate Faculty members, per 4.70.10, and shall coordinate and administer University graduate fellowship and scholarship programs. #16-17-18, #19-20-30. 3.30.15 In carrying out these responsibilities the Dean shall be assisted by the following (see 3.30.16): 3.30.16 The Associate Dean of the Graduate School shall perform the duties of the Dean of the Graduate School during the absence of the Dean and such other duties as are delegated by the Dean. 3.30.17 The Assistant Dean of Graduate Recruitment and Diversity Initiatives shall develop recruitment and retention initiatives to attract and provide support for a diverse population of graduate students and collaborate with departments and colleges to facilitate graduate student success. #16-17-18 New Language 3.30.18 Accelerated Bachelor's and Master's Degrees (ABM). Application and Admission. Students applying for admission into ABM must do so through the URI Graduate School admission system. Applicants must have earned at least 75 credits before they are eligible to apply. Students will be enrolled in ABM after they have met all Graduate School admission requirements, and completed 90 undergraduate credits. 3.30.19 Credit Requirements. Only students accepted into the ABM program will be able to double count credits towards both the bachelor's and master's degrees. The total number of credits that will be allowed to be double counted is up to one-third of the total credits required in the master's

program. Only 500-level courses and 400-level courses designated for graduate credit are eligible to be double counted. 3.30.20 Credits Taken Outside of a program or from another department. Students can transfer credits between URI programs and departments. Only credits earned at URI may be counted toward the master's portion of the ABM. 3.30.21 Time-to-degree Limit. Students must complete all graduate degree requirements for an ABM within the time limit designated by the Graduate School. 3.30.22 Proposals for New ABM Programs. Proposals for new ABM Programs should be submitted to the Faculty Senate Curriculum and Standards Committee after securing approval from the College in which the ABM will be housed. Upon approval of the Curriculum and Standards Committee, the proposal will be forward to the Graduate School. The New Program Committee of the Graduate Council will review the proposal and make a recommendation on its merits to the full Graduate Council. If approved by vote of the Graduate Council, it will be submitted to the Faculty Senate for review and approval as a joint Curriculum and Standards and Graduate Council report.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2025-2026-03 November 20, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Approved by CASC 6/16/25 Approved by FSEC10/1/25 Rationale: URI's “Second Grade Option' (UM S8.33.32; SGO hereafter) allows students at the beginning of their URI career to retake courses in which they received a C- or below.
When they do so, the original grade remains on their transcript but is not used in QPA calculations.
The only exception to this rule occurs when determining whether students are eligible to graduate with distinction (≥3.3 cum laude, ≥3.5 magna cum laude, ≥3.7 summa cum laude).
The QPA to determine eligibility for this honor is calculated using ALL courses taken at the university, including any repeated using the SGO, rather than the QPA printed on the student's transcript.
This results in some students who exercised the SGO being ineligible for honors despite having a suitable QPA. on their transcript.
The argument for the current approach is comparing two students with the same QPA, one of whom exercised their rights to a SGO and the other who did not, the latter student is more deserving of graduation with distinction than the former.

Put another way, students wishing to graduate with distinction should be held to a ‘higher standard' than the transcript-listed QPA.
Jack Humphrey, the registrar, notes, “My research regarding the history of including all courses alt tempted at the University dates back to the 70's.
There was a concern that by not counting all attempts, academic honors could be awarded on an unequal basis (those that utilized the 2nd grade option could be given the academic honors as students that did not have any courses that qualified for the 2nd grade option).

In addition, since the 2nd grade option is not mandatory, it could disenfranchise students who chose to not exercise the 2nd grade option who would have otherwise qualified for academic honors had they chosen to use the 2nd grade option at the start of their undergraduate academic career My concern if we were to eliminate calculating distinction without taking into account all course attempts would be that distinction at commencement would become less meaningful." There was also concern changing the current policy might affect students who, although initially dismissed from URI for poor grades, significantly improved their academic performance after being readmitted under the ^conditional read mission' program (UM $8.25.13 - 8.25.16). the policy might increase their chances of earning this distinction.
There are two arguments against the current approach.
First, both the SGO and conditional read mission program provide a measure of forgiveness for mistakes made early in a student's career; the same principle should apply to studcnts’ ability to graduate with distinction.

Second, many students logically assume that the transcript-listed QPA determines eligibility -- the fact that it does not is confusing and engenders hard feelings in soon-to-be-alumni.
We ask the Faculty Senate to consider eliminating the sentence in s8.22.40 *Distinction* that specifies the QPA for graduating with distinction is calculated using all courses attempted at URI.
Its deletion would mean that student eligibility for graduating cum/ magna/summa laude would by default be determined using the transcript-listed QPA.
This would eliminate student confusion over their eligibility and ensure that the forgiveness embodied in the SGO and conditional read mission policies applies throughout a student's time at the university.

Among comparable New England public institutions,URI alone restricts the timeframe for course repeats and requires the submission of additional paperwork.
Within Rhode Island, Rhode Island College and the Community College of Rhode Island allow any course to be repeated and automatically use the second grade earned in a course in GPA calculations.
Similar policies can be found at other New England public universities (UCONN, UNH, UMASS, UVM, UMaine).
URI itself temporarily expanded use of the SGO during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020but reverted to the existing policy afterwards.

Using longitudinal administrative data from a four-year public institution that alternated between two grading schemes over a short period of seven years, Jiang et al. (2021) found that the adoption of the grade forgiveness policy, over the traditional practice of grade averaging, nudges students to pursue curriculum and/or degrees perceived as relatively more challenging and/or with harder grading standards, such as those in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM).
They also found no evidence that grade forgiveness delayed graduation or reduced student effort.
Contention around excessive course repetition may cause significant disruptions to a student outcomes such as time to degree completion (Jiang et al. 2021; Marx & Meeler 2013).
The latter study also reports that grade forgiveness may also place an unforeseen social or financial burden on students and create challenges with course enrollment.These arguments, along with others, are ultimately empirical questions that prior work has not fully addressed and can be unique to specific institutions.

Considerations to change grade forgiveness policies can affect student achievement and propensities to explore and experiment with different majors, and as a result, may have a substantial impact on the distribution of desirable majors and career fields that are increasingly in high demand (Jiang et al.2021; Stine brick ner & Stine brick ner2014).Morel(2023) found hidden and“credential cartels”that limit thenumber of underrepresented students incertain majors based on GPA requirements and “secondary admissions processes." Jiang et al. (2021) found that grade forgiveness can have a positive impact on degree attainment in STEM fields for the ‘general population of students,” however, “it is not particularly effective in closing the existing gender, income, or racial gaps in these fields" (p.33).

In an effort to increase access to majors and degree programs with second admissions criteria (GPA, credits, etc.), increase the autonomy of student choice of major, advance opportunities for future curriculum changes and path forks, honor flexibility for repeating unproductive grades within reason, and close the major choices of underrepresented populations, the Student Resources sub-group of the URI Student Success Team recommends considerations

to a modified Second Grade Option policy at the University of Rhode Island.

The SGO option is limited to courses taken in the first thirty credits of their URI career; 2.Students must obtain approval from their academic dean and submit a form to the Officeof Enrollment Services each time they intend to employ the SGO.
